rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Modules 2.1 Hydroponics 2.2 Refinery 2.3 Component Shops 2.4 Laboratory 2.5 Constructor 2.6 Reactor 2.7 Splicing Lab 2.8 Workers Lounge 2.9 Private Perk Modules 3 Components 3.1 Brain 3.2 Claw 3.3 Leaves 3.4 Tentacles Overview In Chimera Station, players take turns placing their alien workers on modules. When all are placed, players feed their workers (one food per worker), then take them back to set up for another round. The goal is to get the most points, and points can be earned by building modules, fulfilling conditions on perks, and taking a special Command Modules action. Modules Players can take turns placing one worker on a module. These can include: Hydroponics Gain 2 food, for feeding your workers at the end of the round Refinery Gain 3 money, for buying worker components and modules Component Shops Gain up to 2 components of one type. There's one shop of each type. It's also possible to gain food or coins instead if you have the right type of component on the worker. Laboratory Detach a component from a worker here to move up one space on your research track. This can give a perk, an extra worker, or other benefits. Constructor Pick a module from the reactor at the bottom of the board. Pay its cost in coins, place it on a board space adjacent to an existing module, and gain the bonus on the board from the space selected. You may also move your worker there and activate its action if possible. Reactor Refilling the Reactor will give the reward listed on the right most empty space (after module tiles slide to the right), as well as an extra bonus if an upgraded worker is used. (See Boiler Room in the rules for more info.) Splicing Lab Add components you've obtained previously to the alien worker placed here. Keep in mind a worker can have a maximum of two components, but you can both detach and attach components as needed here. Workers Lounge Gain one coin or one food. This is generally a weaker action, but can be useful if you need food or coins. Any number of workers can visit this space. Private Perk Modules Players may obtain private modules when the obtain a perk. These modules are only usable by the player who has that perk. See Perk Modules in the rules for examples. Components Components are the upgrades you can use to improve your workers. They can be bought from the shops on the right side, and attached through the Splicing Lab, but there are other ways to buy and attach them as well. Brain At least one: Worker also scores module's point value the worker uses With both: When taking a Command Modules action, count all workers instead of only opponents' workers. (See Command Hub modules for more info.) Claw At least one: Worker can move to a space occupied by an opponent's zero or one component worker. With both: Worker can move to a space occupied by any opponent's worker. The worker previously occupying the space moves to the worker's lounge, and its owner gets 1 coin or 1 food. Note some spaces prevent displacement such as the Workers Lounge and Splicing Lab. Leaves At least one: Worker does not need food during the feeding phase With both: Worker also produces two food. Tentacles At least one: When worker collects coin(s) and/or food, increase the amount collected of each by one. With both: When worker collects component(s), increase the amount collected by one (scoring 2 points for each not collected)

[Rating: 1/10] I honestly hated this game. It was more complicated to learn than was necessary, and there were too many options on the board which slowed down the game significantly in a 2 player game.   I would never agree to play this again.

[Rating: 1/10] I've been wanting to try this game for very long, and I'm sad to have to leave such a bad review here because I know many people from the publisher in person. So I apologize in advance for the rant about to come. But I feel like I have to say something, because this was the single worst gaming experience I've ever had in my life.   This game has it all: excruciating analysis paralysis with players who are prone to it, overpowered action spots, broken cards, dreadful and inconsistent iconography which forces you to grab the rulebook every time a new tiles comes out, a high luck factor, ... but 

[Rating: 1/10] Cute twist on worker placement with the customizable workers, but is otherwise utterly unremarkable and boring to play.

[Rating: 1/10] standard Euro game. The splicing of your alien workers is cute, but otherwise, yeah, standard stuff

[Rating: 2/10] Edit: we played a rule wrong about moving the first player, which could possibly improve the experience. However, there were so many other things I disliked about the game that it still doesn't entice me back.  Almost defies every principle of what I consider a fun game. The game is not balanced for four players, but the designer clearly has little idea of balance anyway. I assume he went with the philosophy of if everything is broken, nothing is broken. [Rating: 3/10] The idea is neat, but the game just bored me. There's nothing interesting to it, despite the option to generate different workers (that ain't so different in the end). It's all about getting food and points in a boring way.  When it comes to the components, I doubt that those plastic tiles will survive for a long time.

[Rating: 3/10] What can I say, this game isn't balanced at all, it has too many fiddly rules that come up every 5 mins, you stumble in points, so much so that sometimes making 8 points makes you feel you did nothing.  Some tiles and perks are way more powerful than others, and not all players have the same opportunity to grab them. It seems that it wasn't tested enough.  When we started the game, we knew after the first round who was going to win.   It's cute. It has a few nice ideas. But likely won't play this ever again.

[Rating: 3/10] First off, I don't like games where I need to feed my people, so this game already started on the wrong foot for me.  Add to that the fact that I didn't really care for what you were trying to do in the game, which made for such an ordinary and forgettable experience, that we abandoned the game before the end.

[Rating: 3/10] A game in which its main feature is practically not used. Upgraded workers with tentacles, leaves, brains and claws? No, thanks, I will score more by exchanging them on science, which give me more workers and victory points. And no one can stop me, because there is only one science slot in game. And whoever has the most workers wins.

[Rating: 3/10] 2023-01-17 Rating after first play: 3 Once the novelty of the dolls wear off you see that this is pretty standard modern euro worker placement stuff, that eventuelly breaks down under the weight of added complexity with increasing number of workers, worker powers and worker spots (like these games often do). And after a while the dolls get irritating, as you sometimes have to use force to connect or remove body parts. On the plus side it´s easy to see what modifications your opponents got for their dolls, and going last in turn order can be a huge advantage late-game.  The rules felt ambigious

[Rating: 3.5/10] Rather silly and inflexible worker-placement. The idea of 'modding' workers is good; the execution of this is not.

[Rating: 4/10] I like the idea behind the game, but I feel like there's better worker placement games.  It's not appropriate for solo play.  I think the pieces that get assembled together are a little flimsy.  I found it was easier to not use the heads at all.
